summary: The IPv6 header is a fixed 40-byte header with a 128-bit source and destination address, an 8-bit hop limit, a Next Header field and no checksum or fragmentation fields. Optional features moved into a chain of extension headers that most routers never read. The simpler layout lets hardware forward at line rate, and the 128-bit address space ends the shortage that forced NAT on IPv4. You see it in every dual-stack network, mobile carrier and cloud, and interviewers love to compare it field by field with IPv4.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: IPv6 (RFC 8200) was designed to fix IPv4's address exhaustion and to make routing cheaper. The base header was streamlined: it has a fixed size so a router can find the destination address at a constant offset, it drops the header checksum so no per-hop recomputation is needed, and it removes in-flight fragmentation so routers do not have to buffer and split packets. Everything optional went into extension headers placed between the base header and the transport header, each introduced by the Next Header field of the one before it. The result is a header twice as large as IPv4's minimum but with fewer fields: 8 in total against IPv4's 12 fixed ones.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
bullets: **Version (4 bits)**: always 6.
**Traffic Class (8 bits)**: same role as the IPv4 DSCP and ECN byte: 6 bits of DSCP, 2 bits of ECN.
**Flow Label (20 bits)**: labels packets of one flow so routers can load-balance by flow without parsing ports (RFC 6437). 0 means unlabeled.
**Payload Length (16 bits)**: bytes after the 40-byte base header, including extension headers. Max 65,535 unless a jumbogram is used.
**Next Header (8 bits)**: type of the header that follows, either an extension header or a transport protocol. Shares the IPv4 protocol number space: 6 TCP, 17 UDP, 58 ICMPv6.
**Hop Limit (8 bits)**: TTL by another name, decremented at every router; zero means drop and send ICMPv6 Time Exceeded.
**Source and Destination Address (128 bits each)**: written as eight groups of four hex digits, with `::` compressing one run of zeros.
**Extension header**: an optional header such as hop-by-hop, routing, fragment or destination options. Multiples of 8 bytes in length.
**Path MTU**: the smallest link MTU on the route. IPv6 requires every link to support at least 1280 bytes.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.body: A host builds the 40-byte header, sets Next Header to the transport protocol (or the first extension header), and sends the packet. A router reads the Hop Limit and Destination Address, decrements the Hop Limit, does a longest-prefix lookup and forwards. It never touches the extension chain, except the Hop-by-Hop Options header which, if present, must be first and is examined by every router. If a packet is bigger than the next link's MTU, the router does not fragment: it drops the packet and returns ICMPv6 Packet Too Big (type 2) with the MTU. The sender then lowers its packet size, or inserts a Fragment header and fragments itself. The destination processes the extension headers in order and finally hands the payload to the transport protocol named by the last Next Header. The 40-byte layout is easy to parse. The code below reads the first word, extracts version, traffic class and flow label with shifts, and walks the extension header chain until it reaches a transport protocol. The walk matters for security devices: they must follow every Next Header, because an attacker can hide the TCP header behind many extension headers. Each generic extension header begins with Next Header and Hdr Ext Len (length in 8-byte units not counting the first 8), except the Fragment header, which is a fixed 8 bytes, and AH, whose length is in 4-byte units.

sections.heading: Variants & Types
bullets: **Hop-by-Hop Options (0)**: processed by every router. Used for router alert and jumbograms. Must come first.
**Routing (43)**: source routing. Type 0 was deprecated for amplification attacks (RFC 5095); type 2 supports Mobile IPv6 and type 4 is Segment Routing (SRv6).
**Fragment (44)**: 8 bytes with a 13-bit offset in 8-byte units, an M flag and a 32-bit identification. Only sources fragment.
**Destination Options (60)**: processed by the final destination, or by each routing-list destination when placed before a routing header.
**Authentication Header (51) and ESP (50)**: IPsec headers, built into IPv6 design though now optional.
**No Next Header (59)**: nothing follows; the packet ends here.
**ICMPv6 (58)**: error reporting plus Neighbor Discovery, Router Advertisements and Multicast Listener Discovery. It is essential, unlike ICMP for IPv4.
**Address types**: unicast (global `2000::/3`, link-local `fe80::/10`, unique local `fc00::/7`), multicast `ff00::/8`, anycast (a unicast address in several places). There is no broadcast.

sections.heading: Complexity & Costs
bullets: **Header size**: 40 bytes always, versus 20 to 60 for IPv4. Tunneling or UDP with IPv6 costs 20 extra bytes per packet.
**TCP MSS on 1500 MTU**: 1500 minus 40 minus 20 = 1440 bytes, versus 1460 in IPv4.
**Minimum link MTU**: 1280 bytes. A path MTU below this needs link-layer fragmentation.
**Address space**: 2^128, about 3.4 x 10^38 addresses. A standard end-site subnet is a /64 holding 2^64 interface identifiers.
**Per-hop work**: no checksum to update and no fragmentation, so forwarding is a Hop Limit decrement and a lookup. Extension headers beyond HBH are ignored by transit routers.

**Extension header size**: each is a multiple of 8 bytes. Long chains risk spilling past the first fragment and past hardware parsing limits, which is why many devices drop packets with more than a few headers.
**Jumbogram**: payload up to 4 GB using the Hop-by-Hop Jumbo Payload option with Payload Length set to 0.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls & Gotchas
bullets: **Blocking ICMPv6**: breaks Path MTU Discovery, Neighbor Discovery and autoconfiguration. Drop selected types only, never all of ICMPv6.
**Treating it like IPv4**: there is no header checksum, so the UDP checksum is mandatory (RFC 8200). A UDP packet with checksum 0 is invalid over IPv6.
**Pseudo-header**: TCP, UDP and ICMPv6 checksums cover a pseudo-header that includes the 128-bit source and destination, the upper-layer length and the next header value.
**Extension header ordering**: HBH first, destination options before routing, fragment after routing, upper layer last. Bad ordering is dropped.
**Fragment loss amplification**: only the first fragment has the transport header, so firewalls cannot filter later fragments by port.
**Using a subnet smaller than /64**: breaks SLAAC and some neighbor features, except /127 for point-to-point and /128 for loopbacks.
**Textual ambiguity**: `::` may appear only once in an address, leading zeros inside a group are optional, and `::1` is loopback.
**Traffic class vs flow label confusion**: one marks priority, the other marks flows. Routers must not reorder packets within a flow.

sections.heading: Real-World Use
bullets: **Mobile and ISPs**: most mobile carriers are IPv6-first and reach IPv4 through NAT64 and DNS64 or 464XLAT.
**Cloud and data centers**: dual-stack load balancers, and SRv6 uses the routing header to steer traffic through service chains.
**Local networks**: link-local `fe80::` addresses are on every interface and drive routing protocol neighbors, with SLAAC for host addresses.
**Adoption**: roughly half of traffic to large content networks is IPv6 by the mid-2020s.
**Security tooling**: firewalls must parse the extension chain; RA Guard and DHCPv6 Shield protect LANs from rogue router advertisements.
**Packet capture**: Wireshark filters `ipv6.hlim`, `ipv6.nxt`, `ipv6.fraghdr`.

sections.heading: Interview Notes
bullets: **How big is the IPv6 header?** 40 bytes, fixed, no options in the base header.
**What disappeared compared with IPv4?** Header checksum, IHL, fragmentation fields in the base header, options, and broadcast.
**Who fragments in IPv6?** Only the source host, using a Fragment header after learning the path MTU. Routers never fragment.
**What is the minimum MTU?** 1280 bytes for every link, and 1500 is typical.
**What replaced TTL?** Hop Limit, same behavior with a clearer name.
**What are extension headers?** Chained headers between the base header and transport, identified through Next Header.
**What replaced broadcast?** Multicast, such as the all-nodes address `ff02::1`.

sections.body: An IPv6 address is eight 16-bit groups in hex separated by colons. Leading zeros in a group may be dropped, and the longest run of all-zero groups may be replaced once by `::`. So `2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329` becomes `2001:db8::ff00:42:8329`. Prefix notation matches CIDR: `2001:db8:abcd::/48` is a 48-bit prefix. Addresses in URLs are put in brackets, `http://[2001:db8::1]:8080/`, and a zone id selects an interface for link-local addresses, `fe80::1%eth0`. RFC 5952 recommends lowercase hex and the shortest form, choosing the first run when two runs tie.

subtopics.title: Address types and scopes
subtopics.summary: Global, link-local, unique local and multicast.

sections.body: A host usually has several addresses at once: a link-local one, one or more global ones and temporary privacy addresses.
bullets: **Loopback** `::1`, **unspecified** `::`, **default route** `::/0`.
**Global unicast** `2000::/3`, assigned by registries; documentation prefix `2001:db8::/32`.
**Link-local** `fe80::/10`: valid on one link only, never routed, mandatory on every interface.
**Unique local** `fc00::/7` (in practice `fd00::/8`): private-like, site scoped, no NAT needed.
**Multicast** `ff00::/8`: scope nibble picks link (2), site (5) or global (e); `ff02::1` all nodes, `ff02::2` all routers.
**Solicited-node** `ff02::1:ff00:0/104` plus the low 24 bits of the unicast address, used for Neighbor Discovery.

sections.body: Traffic Class is the DSCP plus ECN byte exactly as in IPv4, so QoS policies carry over. The 20-bit Flow Label is new: a source sets the same non-zero label, with the same source and destination addresses, for all packets of a flow. Routers and load balancers can hash on (source, destination, flow label) to keep one flow on one path without reading transport ports, which is helpful when ports are hidden by encryption or buried behind extension headers. Intermediate routers must not change the label unless they are the originator, and sources should pick the label pseudo-randomly.

Hop-by-Hop Options are the only extension header every router must read, and for that reason many vendors process it on the slow path or drop it, which has made it unreliable on the Internet. Routing headers carry a list of waypoints. Type 0 allowed a single packet to bounce between two routers many times, so it was deprecated; type 2 supports Mobile IPv6 home addresses; type 3 is RPL for low-power networks; type 4 is the Segment Routing Header used by SRv6 to encode a path as a list of 128-bit segment identifiers.

The Fragment header is 8 bytes: Next Header, 8 reserved bits, a 13-bit offset in 8-byte units, 2 reserved bits, the M flag and a 32-bit identification. The part before the fragment header (base header plus any headers that must be processed by routers) is the unfragmentable part and is copied into each fragment; the rest is the fragmentable part. A sender learns the MTU from ICMPv6 Packet Too Big, which is why blocking it is harmful. The reassembly timeout is 60 seconds. Every link must support 1280 bytes, so a sender that cannot learn the MTU can safely use 1280-byte packets.

SLAAC lets a host build its own address from a /64 prefix in a Router Advertisement plus a 64-bit interface identifier. The older EUI-64 method derived the identifier from the MAC by inserting `ff:fe` in the middle and flipping the U/L bit: `00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e` becomes `021a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e`. It leaks the hardware identity, so modern systems use stable opaque identifiers (RFC 7217) and rotating temporary addresses (RFC 8981). Before using any address the host runs Duplicate Address Detection with a Neighbor Solicitation. DHCPv6 is the stateful alternative and is often used with RAs for DNS information.

bullets: **Version**: kept, value 6.
**IHL**: removed, header is a fixed 40 bytes.
**DSCP/ECN**: kept as Traffic Class.
**Total Length**: becomes Payload Length (excludes the base header).
**Identification, Flags, Fragment Offset**: moved to the Fragment extension header.
**TTL**: renamed Hop Limit.
**Protocol**: renamed Next Header and also names extension headers.
**Header Checksum**: removed.
**Options**: replaced by extension headers.
**Addresses**: 32 bits grow to 128 bits.
**New**: Flow Label.

sections.body: Dual stack runs both protocols on every device and is the preferred approach. Tunnels such as 6in4 carry IPv6 inside IPv4 using protocol number 41. NAT64 translates between IPv6-only clients and IPv4 servers, with DNS64 synthesizing AAAA records in the prefix `64:ff9b::/96` that embed the IPv4 address in the last 32 bits. 464XLAT lets IPv4-only apps on a phone work on an IPv6-only carrier. Happy Eyeballs (RFC 8305) races IPv6 and IPv4 connection attempts so a broken path in one family does not delay the user.

takeaways: The IPv6 base header is a fixed 40 bytes: version, traffic class, flow label, payload length, next header, hop limit and two 128-bit addresses.
There is no header checksum, no IHL and no in-flight fragmentation, which keeps router work minimal.
Optional features live in extension headers chained through Next Header; only Hop-by-Hop is read by every router.
Only the source fragments, using a Fragment header, after ICMPv6 Packet Too Big; every link must carry at least 1280 bytes.
UDP checksums are mandatory over IPv6, and TCP, UDP and ICMPv6 checksums cover a pseudo-header with the 128-bit addresses.
Broadcast is gone: multicast (ff02::1 all nodes) and anycast cover it.
Do not block ICMPv6: PMTUD, Neighbor Discovery and SLAAC depend on it.
